units.blurb: Putting the words back into a real headline.

concepts.caption: Prices get bought up hard after a stretch of falling.
concepts.definition: A sustained upward move in price after a period of decline.
concepts.example: Oil prices rallied 4% after the supply cut was announced.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A rally is buyers pushing prices up; a selloff is sellers pushing them down.

concepts.caption: Everyone sells at once and prices get slammed.
concepts.definition: A sharp price drop driven by a wave of selling in a short window.
concepts.example: A global bond selloff pushed yields to a multi-year high.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A selloff drives prices down; a rally drives them up.

concepts.caption: A heavy fall, and it does not stop at one day.
concepts.definition: A large decline in price or volume that usually persists.
concepts.example: India's 10-year bond fell for the 10th straight week in a record slump.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A slump keeps going down; a rebound bounces back up.

concepts.caption: Prices bounce back up after hitting a bottom.
concepts.definition: A recovery in price after a decline, usually short-lived.
concepts.example: AI stocks rebounded after a bruising selloff.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A rebound comes after a fall; a slump is still falling.

concepts.caption: Worse than a selloff — disorderly, almost no buyers.
concepts.definition: A panicked, disorderly market decline.
concepts.example: After this month's Treasury rout, bank shares fell sharply.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A rout is more violent than a selloff: it carries panic and disorder.

concepts.caption: Winners start selling, so the price cools off.
concepts.definition: Selling a position that is in profit, pulling the price down from a high.
concepts.example: Copper hit a two-week low on profit-taking as supply concerns eased.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Profit-taking is voluntary cashing out; a selloff is panic or forced selling.

concepts.caption: How much is actually available to sell.
concepts.definition: The quantity of a good or asset producers are willing to offer at a given price.
concepts.example: Iron ore fell amid concerns over weak demand and rising supply.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Supply is what sellers bring; demand is what buyers want. Opposite ends of one axis.

concepts.caption: How much buyers are willing to pay for.
concepts.definition: The quantity of a good or asset buyers are willing to purchase at a given price.
concepts.example: Analysts expect refined fuel demand will rise 2.5 million bpd.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Demand is buyers wanting in; supply is sellers offering out.

concepts.caption: The most you could produce — not what you did produce.
concepts.definition: The maximum output a facility can reach at full utilisation.
concepts.example: Net capacity adds only 1.2 million bpd over three years.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Capacity is the ceiling; output is what actually came out. They differ when plants sit idle.

concepts.caption: How much actually got produced.
concepts.definition: The quantity actually produced in a given period.
concepts.example: BHP could lift copper output by up to 40% by 2035.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Output is actual production; capacity is the maximum possible.

concepts.caption: Goods made but not yet sold.
concepts.definition: Stock held by a business: raw materials, work in progress and finished goods.
concepts.example: Copper falls as rising inventories ease supply concerns.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Inventory is accumulated stock; output is what a period produced. Stock builds up, output does not.

concepts.caption: The part left over.
concepts.definition: The amount by which supply exceeds demand, or income exceeds spending.
concepts.example: Aluminium is poised for a surplus in 2027 as the supply shock fades.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A surplus is extra; a deficit is a shortfall. Two ends of one scale.

concepts.caption: The part that is missing.
concepts.definition: The amount by which spending exceeds income, or demand exceeds supply.
concepts.example: The country faces a widening fiscal deficit.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A deficit is the gap; a surplus is the leftover.

concepts.caption: The money a company actually made, usually per quarter.
concepts.definition: Net profit after costs over a period, typically reported quarterly.
concepts.example: BHP posted better-than-expected annual earnings.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Earnings are what is left after costs; revenue is the top line before costs.

concepts.caption: Money taken in from sales, before any costs.
concepts.definition: Total income from selling goods or services, before deducting costs.
concepts.example: Randstad revenue exceeded expectations as labour markets improved.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Revenue is the gross take; earnings are what survives the costs.

concepts.caption: What is left after every cost comes out.
concepts.definition: The amount remaining after all costs and expenses are deducted from revenue.
concepts.example: Blackstone's profit fell as volatile markets curbed investment exits.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Profit is an amount; margin is the share of revenue that profit represents.

concepts.caption: How much of each dollar of sales survives as profit.
concepts.definition: Profit as a percentage of revenue — a measure of profitability, not size.
concepts.example: Higher funding costs are starting to affect margins.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Margin is a ratio; profit is an amount. A small company can have a fat margin.

concepts.caption: A slice of profit paid out to shareholders.
concepts.definition: A cash or stock distribution paid to shareholders out of profit.
concepts.example: BHP declared a final dividend of 99 cents per share.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Earnings are what the company made; a dividend is the slice handed to shareholders.

concepts.caption: The company's own official expectation, not a result.
concepts.definition: Management's official expectation for future performance.
concepts.example: Santos trimmed the upper end of its production guidance.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Guidance is the company's own official number; a forecast can come from anyone about anything.

concepts.caption: An estimate of what comes next — anyone's counts.
concepts.definition: An estimate of future conditions based on current information.
concepts.example: HSBC is forecast to show a 33% increase in pretax profit.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A forecast is the broader idea; guidance is specifically the company's own official outlook.

concepts.caption: Many analysts' forecasts averaged into one number.
concepts.definition: The average of analysts' estimates, used as the bar for beating or missing.
concepts.example: BHP surpassed the consensus estimate of $12.66 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Consensus is everyone blended together; an estimate is one person's number.

concepts.caption: One specific number, usually from one analyst.
concepts.definition: An individual approximation of a value.
concepts.example: The consensus estimate was $12.66 billion.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An estimate is one number; consensus is the average of many.

concepts.caption: An IOU: you lend, they pay interest, you get principal back.
concepts.definition: A debt security issued by a government or company, paying interest and repaying principal at maturity.
concepts.example: Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A bond is the certificate; yield is the return it pays at the price you bought it.

concepts.caption: What an investment pays you each year, at your purchase price.
concepts.definition: Investment return relative to price paid; bond yields rise when prices fall.
concepts.example: The benchmark yield settled at 7.4427%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Yield is a return rate; a bond is the instrument. Prices fall, yields rise.

concepts.caption: The same money buys less than it used to.
concepts.definition: A sustained rise in the general price level, eroding purchasing power.
concepts.example: September consumer inflation quickened to 5.54%.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Inflation is the problem itself — prices climbing; the interest rate is the tool used against it.

concepts.caption: The price of borrowing, and the central bank's main tool.
concepts.definition: The cost of borrowing as a percentage of principal, steered by the policy rate.
concepts.example: All three central banks are expected to leave rates unchanged.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An interest rate is the price of borrowing; a yield is what you earn by holding an investment.

concepts.caption: The central bank pushes rates up.
concepts.definition: A central bank increase in the policy interest rate.
concepts.example: Swap markets are pricing in about 100 basis points of rate hikes.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A hike moves rates up; a cut moves them down.

concepts.caption: The central bank pulls rates down.
concepts.definition: A central bank reduction in the policy interest rate.
concepts.example: Investors expect a rate cut next quarter.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A cut moves rates down; a hike moves them up.

concepts.caption: The institution that sets money supply and rates.
concepts.definition: The authority responsible for monetary policy, money supply and interest rates.
concepts.example: Traders awaited minutes from the central bank's latest meeting.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The central bank is the institution; the interest rate is the dial it turns.

concepts.caption: The money a country or region circulates.
concepts.definition: The means of payment issued and enforced by a government.
concepts.example: The rupiah fell to a three-month low as Asian currencies struggled.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Currency is the money itself; the exchange rate is the ratio between two of them.

concepts.caption: How much of one currency buys another.
concepts.definition: The rate at which one currency converts into another.
concepts.example: Changing foreign-exchange conditions are putting earnings at risk.
concepts.mixUpWhy: The exchange rate is the ratio; currency is the thing being exchanged.

concepts.caption: Your money buys less foreign currency than before.
concepts.definition: A fall in one currency's value against another.
concepts.example: The Taiwan dollar depreciated against the US dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Depreciate means cheaper; appreciate means more valuable.

concepts.caption: Your money buys more foreign currency than before.
concepts.definition: A rise in one currency's value against another.
concepts.example: China's yuan hit its highest level since 2022 on a weaker dollar.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Appreciate means more valuable; depreciate means cheaper.

concepts.caption: What the whole company is worth on the stock market.
concepts.definition: Share price multiplied by shares outstanding — the market's total price for the company.
concepts.example: Its market cap makes it the largest listed mining company.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Market cap is the price the market sets; valuation is the judgment of what it should be worth.

concepts.caption: What something is judged to be worth.
concepts.definition: An assessment or calculation of an asset's or company's intrinsic worth.
concepts.example: Analysts flagged stretched valuations in the energy sector.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Valuation is a judgement of worth; market cap is the total price the market currently assigns.

concepts.caption: The share price as a multiple of yearly profit per share.
concepts.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share — what investors pay per dollar of profit.
concepts.example: Its P/E ratio is well above the sector average.
concepts.mixUpWhy: P/E is a multiple tied to profit; market cap is a total tied to share count.

concepts.caption: A basket of stocks boiled down to one number.
concepts.definition: A composite measure calculated from a weighted group of assets.
concepts.example: Blue chips headed for the longest weekly losing streak.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An index is a computed number; a blue chip is one of the companies inside it.

concepts.caption: A big, stable, well-known company's stock.
concepts.definition: Shares of a large, financially sound and well-established company.
concepts.example: Chinese stocks slid as blue chips set for the longest losing streak.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A blue chip is a company; an index is many companies combined into a figure.

concepts.caption: Governments and companies sell bonds by competitive bidding.
concepts.definition: A process of issuing or selling assets through competitive bids.
concepts.example: Vietnam raised $371 million in a government bond auction.
concepts.mixUpWhy: An auction is the bidding process; issuance is the act of bringing the securities out.

concepts.caption: The amount of new bonds or shares brought to market.
concepts.definition: The act, or total volume, of issuing new securities.
concepts.example: Bond dealers expect a modest increase in UK debt issuance.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Issuance is bringing securities out; an auction is one way to price them.

concepts.caption: A tax charged when imported goods cross the border.
concepts.definition: A tax imposed on imported goods.
concepts.example: Canadian steelmakers offset some US tariff pain with domestic demand.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A tariff adds cost to imports, which squeezes supply; supply is the quantity available itself.

concepts.caption: How violently the price swings, up or down.
concepts.definition: The magnitude and frequency of price swings over a period.
concepts.example: Greater foreign-exchange volatility is beginning to affect asset quality.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Volatility is how much price swings either way; a selloff is a one-way fall.
